sentence: Which reading of B's comparison is supported?
setupText: A: 'The appendices can wait; only the main report matters.' B: 'The appendices are no less useful than the main report.'
taskText: Which reading of B's comparison is supported?
text: A: 'The appendices can wait; only the main report matters.' B: 'The appendices are no less useful than the main report.' Which reading of B's comparison is supported?
options: B ranks the appendices as slightly less useful than the report.
B says the appendices are useful only when read after the report.
B rejects placing the appendices below the report in usefulness.
B ranks the appendices above the report by a small amount.
answer: B rejects placing the appendices below the report in usefulness.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-781:No less plus adjective denying inferiority
explanation: No less useful denies inferiority on that scale; it counters A's dismissal without requiring that the appendices be superior.

rationales.B rejects placing the appendices below t: No less useful denies inferiority on that scale; it counters A's dismissal without requiring that the appendices be superior.
rationales.B ranks the appendices as slightly less: No negates the lower ranking; it does not merely reduce the size of a disadvantage.
rationales.B says the appendices are useful only wh: The comparison addresses usefulness, not a required reading order.
rationales.B ranks the appendices above the report: They may be equally useful; no less does not require a positive lead.

sentence: Which paraphrase best preserves the strength and direction of the comparison?
setupText: After viewing two charts, a reader says, 'The first isn't nearly as clear as the revised one.'
taskText: Which paraphrase best preserves the strength and direction of the comparison?
text: After viewing two charts, a reader says, 'The first isn't nearly as clear as the revised one.' Which paraphrase best preserves the strength and direction of the comparison?
options: The revised chart is only slightly clearer than the first.
The revised chart is considerably less clear than the first.
The revised chart is considerably clearer than the first.
The revised chart is almost as clear as the first.
answer: The revised chart is considerably clearer than the first.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-782:Not nearly as ... as marking a substantial gap
explanation: Not nearly as ... as places the first well below the revised chart in clarity.

rationales.The revised chart is only slightly clear: Not nearly as clear marks a substantial gap, not just a slight improvement.
rationales.The revised chart is considerably cleare: Not nearly as ... as places the first well below the revised chart in clarity.
rationales.The revised chart is considerably less c: This reverses which chart is clearer.
rationales.The revised chart is almost as clear as: Almost as clear places the revised chart slightly below the first, changing both direction and degree.

sentence: Which editorial comment is accurate?
setupText: In an informal conversation about three rooms, one guest says 'This room is cheapest of the three'; another says 'This room is the cheapest of the three.'
taskText: Which editorial comment is accurate?
text: In an informal conversation about three rooms, one guest says 'This room is cheapest of the three'; another says 'This room is the cheapest of the three.' Which editorial comment is accurate?
options: Only the version with the can express a group ranking.
The bare version compares two rooms; the version with the compares three.
The bare version means very cheap without comparing the rooms.
Both can express the same lowest-price ranking in this context.
answer: Both can express the same lowest-price ranking in this context.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-783:Optional the with an informal predicative superlative
explanation: After is with no following noun, informal English permits the to be omitted here; both versions rank this room lowest in price.

rationales.Only the version with the can express a: A predicative superlative without a following noun can omit the in informal use and still rank the group.
rationales.The bare version compares two rooms; the: The phrase of the three sets the group in both versions; article choice does not change its size.
rationales.Both can express the same lowest-price r: After is with no following noun, informal English permits the to be omitted here; both versions rank this room lowest in price.
rationales.The bare version means very cheap withou: Cheapest and of the three still supply a superlative ranking; omitting the does not turn it into very cheap.

sentence: What role does the diagram have in this comparison?
setupText: The organiser writes, 'The instructions are all the easier to follow for having a diagram.'
taskText: What role does the diagram have in this comparison?
text: The organiser writes, 'The instructions are all the easier to follow for having a diagram.' What role does the diagram have in this comparison?
options: It contributes to making the instructions easier to follow.
It makes every instruction equally easy to follow.
It compensates for instructions that have become harder overall.
It is compared with the instructions as an alternative set of directions.
answer: It contributes to making the instructions easier to follow.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-784:All the plus comparative with a reason
explanation: All the plus a comparative, followed by a reason, presents that reason as adding to the degree described.

rationales.It makes every instruction equally easy: All the easier strengthens an improvement; all does not distribute equal ease across every instruction.
rationales.It compensates for instructions that hav: The phrase attributes increased ease to the diagram; it does not report an overall deterioration.
rationales.It is compared with the instructions as: For having a diagram gives a reason for the increased ease, not a second set of instructions being ranked.
rationales.It contributes to making the instruction: All the plus a comparative, followed by a reason, presents that reason as adding to the degree described.

sentence: Which ranking follows in the ordinary degree reading?
setupText: An adviser says, 'No other form in this packet is as confusing as the registration form.'
taskText: Which ranking follows in the ordinary degree reading?
text: An adviser says, 'No other form in this packet is as confusing as the registration form.' Which ranking follows in the ordinary degree reading?
options: The registration form is more confusing than every other form in the packet.
The registration form ties with at least one other for most confusing.
At least one form is more confusing than the registration form.
The registration form is the most confusing form the adviser has ever seen.
answer: The registration form is more confusing than every other form in the packet.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-785:No other with an equality comparison yielding a unique maximum
explanation: No other form reaches its degree of confusion; the sentence gives it the top position without a tie in this packet.

rationales.The registration form is more confusing: No other form reaches its degree of confusion; the sentence gives it the top position without a tie in this packet.
rationales.The registration form ties with at least: A tied form would be as confusing, which no other excludes.
rationales.At least one form is more confusing than: A more confusing form would exceed the level that no other says any form reaches.
rationales.The registration form is the most confus: The comparison set is this packet, not the adviser's entire experience.

sentence: What does B's reply do?
setupText: A: 'Was the checklist useful?' B: 'More than useful. It prevented us from sending the wrong files.'
taskText: What does B's reply do?
text: A: 'Was the checklist useful?' B: 'More than useful. It prevented us from sending the wrong files.' What does B's reply do?
options: It compares the number of checklists with the number of files.
It contrasts the checklist's usefulness with its accuracy.
It limits the checklist's usefulness to correcting earlier mistakes.
It treats useful as too weak a description of the checklist's value.
answer: It treats useful as too weak a description of the checklist's value.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-786:More than plus adjective as an evaluative upgrade
explanation: More than useful upgrades A's description; the prevented mistake supplies a reason for the stronger praise.

rationales.It compares the number of checklists wit: More than modifies the assessment useful, not a count of objects.
rationales.It treats useful as too weak a descripti: More than useful upgrades A's description; the prevented mistake supplies a reason for the stronger praise.
rationales.It contrasts the checklist's usefulness: No separate quality such as accuracy is introduced as the comparison point.
rationales.It limits the checklist's usefulness to: The example concerns preventing a mistake, and the phrase strengthens rather than restricts the praise.

sentence: Which paraphrase preserves the comparison?
setupText: The technician says, 'The damaged cable is less of a problem than the missing software.'
taskText: Which paraphrase preserves the comparison?
text: The technician says, 'The damaged cable is less of a problem than the missing software.' Which paraphrase preserves the comparison?
options: The cable is damaged to a lesser physical extent than the software.
The missing software presents the greater difficulty.
The cable has fewer individual faults than the software.
The cable is not a problem once the software is installed.
answer: The missing software presents the greater difficulty.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-787:Less of a plus noun grading a category
explanation: Less of a problem grades how serious an issue is; the cable is below the missing software on that scale.

rationales.The cable is damaged to a lesser physica: Less of a problem compares difficulty caused, not the physical extent of damage to each item.
rationales.The cable has fewer individual faults th: The sentence compares overall difficulty, not counts of faults.
rationales.The missing software presents the greate: Less of a problem grades how serious an issue is; the cable is below the missing software on that scale.
rationales.The cable is not a problem once the soft: A smaller problem is still compatible with a problem; the sentence gives no condition that removes it.

sentence: What is the traveller asking about?
setupText: At a ticket desk, a traveller asks, 'Would it be any cheaper to return on Tuesday?'
taskText: What is the traveller asking about?
text: At a ticket desk, a traveller asks, 'Would it be any cheaper to return on Tuesday?' What is the traveller asking about?
options: Which Tuesday service has the lowest price of all services
Whether changing the return day would reduce the price at all
Whether Tuesday's price would be lower by a particular amount
Whether a Tuesday return is cheaper than every other return day
answer: Whether changing the return day would reduce the price at all
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-788:Any modifying a comparative in a question
explanation: Any before cheaper asks whether even some reduction is available, without specifying its size.

rationales.Which Tuesday service has the lowest pri: The question compares the proposed change with the current plan; it does not request a ranking of every Tuesday service.
rationales.Whether Tuesday's price would be lower b: Any cheaper leaves the amount open rather than naming a required saving.
rationales.Whether a Tuesday return is cheaper than: No comparison with every other day is stated.
rationales.Whether changing the return day would re: Any before cheaper asks whether even some reduction is available, without specifying its size.

sentence: Which pattern does the editor describe?
setupText: An editor observes, 'The more detail we add, the less readable the guide becomes.'
taskText: Which pattern does the editor describe?
text: An editor observes, 'The more detail we add, the less readable the guide becomes.' Which pattern does the editor describe?
options: Both detail and readability increase together.
Readability falls as the amount of detail rises.
Detail is being removed because readability has already fallen.
The guide becomes less detailed as readers gain experience.
answer: Readability falls as the amount of detail rises.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-789:Opposing directions in paired comparatives
explanation: The paired comparatives move in opposite directions: more detail accompanies less readability.

rationales.Readability falls as the amount of detai: The paired comparatives move in opposite directions: more detail accompanies less readability.
rationales.Both detail and readability increase tog: Less readable marks a decrease in readability, not an increase.
rationales.Detail is being removed because readabil: The sentence describes adding detail and the associated change, not a decision to remove it.
rationales.The guide becomes less detailed as reade: Neither removal of detail nor readers' experience is the stated changing factor.

sentence: Which sentence achieves that writing goal?
setupText: A profile must give equal weight to Tessa's roles as designer and manager, without claiming how she divides her hours.
taskText: Which sentence achieves that writing goal?
text: A profile must give equal weight to Tessa's roles as designer and manager, without claiming how she divides her hours. Which sentence achieves that writing goal?
options: Tessa spends as much time managing as designing.
Tessa is as much a manager as she is a designer.
Tessa is more a manager than a designer.
Tessa manages as many designers as the other managers do.
answer: Tessa is as much a manager as she is a designer.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-790:As much a ... as comparing roles
explanation: As much a ... as gives the roles equal standing without measuring time spent on them.

rationales.Tessa spends as much time managing as de: This compares hours, which the writing goal explicitly leaves unclaimed.
rationales.Tessa is as much a manager as she is a d: As much a ... as gives the roles equal standing without measuring time spent on them.
More ... than gives the managerial role greater weight rather than equal weight.
rationales.Tessa manages as many designers as the o: This compares staff numbers, not the importance of her two roles.

sentence: Which relationship is asserted?
setupText: An organiser writes, 'More people registered than there are seats in the hall.'
taskText: Which relationship is asserted?
text: An organiser writes, 'More people registered than there are seats in the hall.' Which relationship is asserted?
options: The hall has more seats than registered people.
The number attending exceeds the number registered.
The registration count exceeds the seating capacity.
The hall needs more seats than any other hall.
answer: The registration count exceeds the seating capacity.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-791:A comparative clause comparing counts of unlike entities
explanation: The than-clause supplies the seat count as the standard for the number of people registered.

rationales.The hall has more seats than registered: That reverses which quantity is greater.
rationales.The number attending exceeds the number: The sentence compares registrations with seats, not attendance with registration.
rationales.The registration count exceeds the seati: The than-clause supplies the seat count as the standard for the number of people registered.
rationales.The hall needs more seats than any other: No other hall appears in the comparison.

sentence: Which statement accurately compares the new price with last year's price?
setupText: A pass cost $100 last year and costs $80 this year.
taskText: Which statement accurately compares the new price with last year's price?
text: A pass cost $100 last year and costs $80 this year. Which statement accurately compares the new price with last year's price?
options: This year's price is 80% lower than last year's.
Last year's price was 20% higher than this year's.
This year's price has fallen to 20% of last year's.
This year's price is 20% lower than last year's.
answer: This year's price is 20% lower than last year's.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-792:Percentage comparison and its reference amount
explanation: The decrease is twenty dollars out of the old hundred-dollar price, so the reduction is 20%.

rationales.This year's price is 80% lower than last: Eighty percent lower would leave a twenty-dollar price; eighty dollars is 80% of the old price.
rationales.Last year's price was 20% higher than th: The reverse percentage uses eighty as its base; twenty dollars is 25% of eighty, not 20%.
rationales.This year's price has fallen to 20% of l: To 20% describes a twenty-dollar final price rather than the twenty-dollar decrease.
rationales.This year's price is 20% lower than last: The decrease is twenty dollars out of the old hundred-dollar price, so the reduction is 20%.

sentence: What does this wording allow?
setupText: A shop advertises, 'Selected desks: up to 30% cheaper than last month.'
taskText: What does this wording allow?
text: A shop advertises, 'Selected desks: up to 30% cheaper than last month.' What does this wording allow?
options: Every desk in the shop has a 30% reduction.
Thirty percent is the minimum reduction for selected desks.
Some selected desks may have a reduction smaller than 30%.
The desks now cost 30% of last month's prices.
answer: Some selected desks may have a reduction smaller than 30%.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-793:Up to limiting a comparative discount
explanation: Up to sets an upper limit on the advertised reduction; it does not give every selected desk the maximum discount.

rationales.Some selected desks may have a reduction: Up to sets an upper limit on the advertised reduction; it does not give every selected desk the maximum discount.
rationales.Every desk in the shop has a 30% reducti: Selected restricts the stock, and up to does not promise the maximum for every selected item.
rationales.Thirty percent is the minimum reduction: Up to makes 30% the upper, not the lower, limit.
rationales.The desks now cost 30% of last month's p: Thirty percent cheaper means a reduction from the old price, not a final price equal to 30% of it.

sentence: Which count pair best fits that description?
setupText: A report says the new system processed nearly twice as many requests as the old one under the same test conditions.
taskText: Which count pair best fits that description?
text: A report says the new system processed nearly twice as many requests as the old one under the same test conditions. Which count pair best fits that description?
options: Old: 100 requests; new: 105 requests
Old: 100 requests; new: 195 requests
Old: 100 requests; new: 205 requests
Old: 100 requests; new: 295 requests
answer: Old: 100 requests; new: 195 requests
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-794:Nearly modifying a multiplier comparison
explanation: Nearly twice as many places the new count close to, but below, two times the old count.

rationales.Old: 100 requests; new: 105 requests: That is only slightly more, not close to double.
rationales.Old: 100 requests; new: 195 requests: Nearly twice as many places the new count close to, but below, two times the old count.
rationales.Old: 100 requests; new: 205 requests: This is slightly more than twice as many, not nearly twice in the ordinary below-target reading.
rationales.Old: 100 requests; new: 295 requests: That is nearly three times the old count, not nearly twice.

sentence: What is being compared?
setupText: After a supposed consultation, a resident says, 'It felt more like a sales presentation than a discussion.'
taskText: What is being compared?
text: After a supposed consultation, a resident says, 'It felt more like a sales presentation than a discussion.' What is being compared?
options: The number of sales presentations and discussions held
The resident's preference for presentations over discussions
The meeting's resemblance to two kinds of event
The duration of the sales and discussion portions
answer: The meeting's resemblance to two kinds of event
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-795:More like ... than comparing resemblance
explanation: More like ... than compares how well two descriptions fit the same experience.

rationales.The number of sales presentations and di: More modifies like here, not a count of events.
rationales.The resident's preference for presentati: The sentence characterizes what the meeting resembled; it does not say which event the resident prefers.
rationales.The meeting's resemblance to two kinds o: More like ... than compares how well two descriptions fit the same experience.
rationales.The duration of the sales and discussion: The comparison concerns resemblance, not explicitly the time spent on separate portions.

sentence: How does the edit change the comparison?
setupText: A report calls a design 'the best of the three we tested.' An editor changes this to 'the best possible design.'
taskText: How does the edit change the comparison?
text: A report calls a design 'the best of the three we tested.' An editor changes this to 'the best possible design.' How does the edit change the comparison?
options: It expands the ranking claim beyond the three tested designs.
It limits the claim to designs that passed the test.
It changes the design from best to merely acceptable.
It makes the claim depend only on the most recent test.
answer: It expands the ranking claim beyond the three tested designs.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-796:A bounded superlative versus best possible
explanation: Best of the three is bounded by the tested set; best possible reaches across what could be available or achieved.

rationales.It limits the claim to designs that pass: Best possible does not retain the explicit group of three or add a pass condition.
rationales.It changes the design from best to merel: Both versions use a highest-rank description; the issue is the comparison set, not a downgrade to acceptable.
rationales.It makes the claim depend only on the mo: The edit says nothing about which test occurred most recently.
rationales.It expands the ranking claim beyond the: Best of the three is bounded by the tested set; best possible reaches across what could be available or achieved.

sentence: Which reading best fits this comment?
setupText: After a long absence, a listener says, 'Her playing is as expressive as ever.'
taskText: Which reading best fits this comment?
text: After a long absence, a listener says, 'Her playing is as expressive as ever.' Which reading best fits this comment?
options: Her playing retains the expressive quality the listener remembers.
Her playing has become more expressive than at any earlier time.
Her playing was never expressive before this performance.
Her playing is less expressive than the listener remembers.
answer: Her playing retains the expressive quality the listener remembers.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-797:As ... as ever retaining an established standard
explanation: As expressive as ever presents the familiar degree as continuing, rather than announcing a new improvement or decline.

rationales.Her playing retains the expressive quali: As expressive as ever presents the familiar degree as continuing, rather than announcing a new improvement or decline.
rationales.Her playing has become more expressive t: That would be more expressive than ever; as ... as does not announce a new peak.
rationales.Her playing was never expressive before: As ... as ever invokes an established quality rather than its first appearance.
rationales.Her playing is less expressive than the: The equality comparison does not report a loss of expressiveness.

sentence: What comparison does B make?
setupText: A: 'Should I buy the cheaper printer?' B: 'You'd be better off keeping the old one; these cartridges cost a fortune.'
taskText: What comparison does B make?
text: A: 'Should I buy the cheaper printer?' B: 'You'd be better off keeping the old one; these cartridges cost a fortune.' What comparison does B make?
options: The old printer necessarily produces higher-quality pages.
The old printer has a lower purchase price than the new one.
A could sell the new printer for more than the old one.
Keeping the old printer would put A in a more favorable practical position.
answer: Keeping the old printer would put A in a more favorable practical position.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-798:Better off comparing a person's resulting situation
explanation: Better off compares the person's likely situation under two choices, here with running costs as the reason.

rationales.The old printer necessarily produces hig: Better off evaluates A's situation; the stated reason concerns cartridge costs, not page quality.
rationales.Keeping the old printer would put A in a: Better off compares the person's likely situation under two choices, here with running costs as the reason.
rationales.The old printer has a lower purchase pri: A already owns the old printer, and B's reason concerns cartridges rather than a comparison of purchase prices.
rationales.A could sell the new printer for more th: The reply recommends retaining the old printer; it does not compare resale values.

sentence: What does B convey?
setupText: A: 'Is the repaired scanner any more reliable?' B: 'If anything, it's less reliable now.'
taskText: What does B convey?
text: A: 'Is the repaired scanner any more reliable?' B: 'If anything, it's less reliable now.' What does B convey?
options: Any change B can identify goes toward lower reliability, not improvement.
B confirms a small but clear improvement in reliability.
B says reliability will improve if another repair is made.
B says the scanner's reliability has remained exactly equal.
answer: Any change B can identify goes toward lower reliability, not improvement.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-799:If anything qualifying a contrary comparative
explanation: If anything tentatively directs the comparison toward the opposite of the suggested improvement.

rationales.B confirms a small but clear improvement: Less reliable points toward deterioration, the opposite of improvement.
rationales.B says reliability will improve if anoth: If anything here is not a condition requiring another repair.
rationales.Any change B can identify goes toward lo: If anything tentatively directs the comparison toward the opposite of the suggested improvement.
rationales.B says the scanner's reliability has rem: B favors a negative change, though cautiously; exact equality is not the comparison offered.

sentence: Which situation fits that distinction?
setupText: A city newsletter says, 'The library now stays open three hours later, not three hours longer.'
taskText: Which situation fits that distinction?
text: A city newsletter says, 'The library now stays open three hours later, not three hours longer.' Which situation fits that distinction?
options: The opening time stayed fixed and closing moved three hours later.
Closing stayed fixed and opening moved three hours earlier.
Both opening and closing moved three hours earlier.
Both opening and closing times moved three hours later.
answer: Both opening and closing times moved three hours later.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-b2-800:Later as an endpoint versus longer as a duration
explanation: Moving both endpoints equally shifts the closing time later while leaving the number of open hours unchanged.

rationales.The opening time stayed fixed and closin: That would extend the daily duration by three hours, so longer would also apply.
rationales.Closing stayed fixed and opening moved t: That would make the day longer, but the library would not close later.
rationales.Both opening and closing moved three hou: The duration would stay the same, but closing would be earlier rather than later.
rationales.Both opening and closing times moved thr: Moving both endpoints equally shifts the closing time later while leaving the number of open hours unchanged.
